items.question: Give an account of the three crowned kingdoms (Muvendar) of the Sangam Age, comparing their capitals, ports and notable rulers.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Sangam Age (c. 300 BCE – 300 CE)** in **Tamilakam** was dominated by three crowned dynasties — the **Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas**, collectively the **Muvendar** — each with a distinct emblem, capital and port.

The **Cholas** (emblem: **tiger**) ruled the **Cauvery delta**, extending to parts of **southern Andhra Pradesh** between the Pennar and Vellar rivers. Their capitals were **Uraiyur** (famed for cotton) and the port **Kaveripattinam (Puhar)**. Their greatest ruler, **Karikala**, won the **Battle of Venni** against a Chera–Pandya confederacy and built the **Kallanai Dam (Grand Anicut)** across the Cauvery, promoting irrigation and making Puhar a centre of Roman trade.

The **Cheras** (emblem: **bow**) ruled **Kerala and western Tamil Nadu** from **Vanji (Karur)**, with ports **Muziris** and **Tondi** handling Roman trade. **Cheran Senguttuvan** led a Himalayan expedition and founded the **Pattini Cult** of Kannagi; his contemporaneity with the Sri Lankan king **Gajabahu** (the Gajabahu synchronism) is a key dating anchor.

The **Pandyas** (emblem: **fish**) ruled southern Tamil Nadu from **Madurai** on the Vaigai, with the pearl-fishing port **Korkai**. **Neduncheliyan** (Aryappadai Kadantha) figures in the Silappathikaram, while **Thalaiyalanganaattu Neduncheliyan** won the Battle of Thalaiyalanganam.

Though often at war, the three kingdoms shared a common Tamil culture, patronised the Sangam assemblies, and built a prosperous, trade-linked society before the **Kalabhra** invasion ended the age.
keyPoints: Muvendar = Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas; period c. 300 BCE – 300 CE.
Chola: tiger, Uraiyur/Puhar, Cauvery delta into southern AP; Karikala & Kallanai Dam.
Chera: bow, Vanji (Karur), ports Muziris/Tondi; Senguttuvan & Pattini Cult.
Pandya: fish, Madurai, port Korkai (pearls); Neduncheliyan.
Shared Tamil culture and Sangam patronage; ended by the Kalabhra invasion.

items.question: Discuss Sangam literature as a source for reconstructing the history and society of early Tamilakam.
items.modelAnswer:
**Sangam literature** — produced under royal patronage across the **three Sangam assemblies (Muchchangam)** — is the principal literary source for early South Indian history.

The **Tolkappiyam** (by **Tolkappiyar**), the earliest Tamil grammar, is invaluable beyond linguistics: it describes the **political, social and economic conditions** of the age, including the **five-fold land division (Tinai)** — Kurinji, Mullai, Marudam, Neydal and Palai — each with its own deity and mode of life.

The **Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies)** and **Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls)**, by poets such as Kapilar, Nakkirar and **Avvaiyar**, celebrate love, heroism and the valour of kings, and vividly reflect everyday society, trade and warfare. The **Pathinenkilkanakku (Eighteen Lesser Works)** are didactic; its jewel, the **Tirukkural** of **Thiruvalluvar** (1,330 couplets on Virtue, Wealth and Love), is a timeless ethical classic.

The twin epics deepen the picture: **Silappathikaram** (Ilango Adigal) narrates Kannagi and Kovalan, illuminating polity and the **Pattini Cult**, while **Manimekalai** (Sittalai Sattanar), a **Buddhist epic**, reflects the religious currents of the day.

Used alongside archaeology — **Roman coins**, Arikamedu remains — this literature lets historians reconstruct Sangam **polity, economy, religion and social structure**, though its poetic and idealised character requires cautious, corroborated interpretation.
keyPoints: Sangam literature produced under the three Sangam assemblies.
Tolkappiyam: grammar + political/social/economic data and the Tinai scheme.
Ettuthokai & Pattuppattu on love, heroism and kingship; poets like Avvaiyar.
Tirukkural (Thiruvalluvar): 1,330 couplets on Virtue, Wealth, Love.
Epics Silappathikaram and Manimekalai add polity and religion.
Best used with archaeology (Roman coins, Arikamedu); read critically.

items.question: Examine the economy of the Sangam Age, highlighting the significance of Indo-Roman trade.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Sangam economy** rested on a strong **agrarian base** supplemented by flourishing crafts and long-distance trade.

**Agriculture** was the backbone: **rice** (the staple), sugarcane, cotton, pepper, turmeric, ginger and jackfruit were grown, supported by irrigation tanks, wells and reservoirs. **Karikala Chola's Kallanai Dam** across the Cauvery advanced both irrigation and flood control, while forest reclamation expanded farmland.

**Handicrafts** thrived — weaving (the **cotton textiles of Uraiyur** were prized in Roman markets), metalwork, shipbuilding and bead-making. **Arikamedu** (beads and ceramics), Madurai and Kanchipuram were noted craft centres. **Internal trade** used a **barter system**, with day and night markets (noted in the Maduraikanchi), salt merchants (**Umanar**) and mobile traders (**Chattu**); merchant guilds were called **Nigama**.

**Indo-Roman trade** was the dynamic external element. Ports such as **Puhar, Muziris, Korkai, Arikamedu and Tondi** connected Tamilakam to **Rome, Greece and Southeast Asia**. **Exports** included spices (pepper, turmeric, cardamom), textiles, pearls and ivory; **imports** were **gold, Roman wine and horses**. The abundant **Roman coins** unearthed in Tamil Nadu — used as currency and as ornaments — confirm this trade, whose inflow of gold enriched the economy and spurred the **growth of port cities** and social stratification.

Thus the Sangam economy combined agrarian strength, skilled crafts and vibrant maritime commerce, with Indo-Roman trade acting as a powerful engine of urban prosperity.
keyPoints: Agrarian base: rice staple plus spices, cotton; irrigation and the Kallanai Dam.
Crafts: Uraiyur cotton, metalwork, shipbuilding; Arikamedu a key centre.
Internal trade by barter; Umanar (salt), Chattu (mobile traders), guilds (Nigama).
Ports Puhar, Muziris, Korkai, Arikamedu, Tondi link to Rome/Greece/SE Asia.
Exports spices/textiles/pearls/ivory; imports gold/wine/horses.
Roman coins confirm trade; gold inflow spurred urban growth and stratification.

items.question: Describe the polity and society of the Sangam Age, with reference to administration, the Tinai landscapes and the position of women.
items.modelAnswer:
**Polity.** Sangam government was a **hereditary monarchy**; kings adopted grand titles such as **Thennavar** (Southern King) and **Minavar** (Warrior of the Seas). They were assisted by officials — **Amaichar** (ministers), **Anthanar** (priests), **Senathipathi** (commanders), **Otrar** (spies) and **Thuthar** (envoys). The realm was graded into **Mandalam** (province) → **Nadu** (district) → **Ur** (town) → **Perur** and **Sirur** (villages), with coastal trade towns called **Pattinam** and artisan suburbs called **Cheri**. Revenue came from **Karai** (land tax), **Ulgu** (customs), **Irai** (tribute) and **Iravu** (extra demand), besides **war booty**; each king kept a standing army with distinctive banners (**Kodimaram**).

**Society.** The **Tolkappiyam** describes a **five-fold landscape (Tinai)** — **Kurinji** (hills, Murugan, hunting), **Mullai** (pastoral, Vishnu, herding), **Marudam** (agricultural, Indra, farming), **Neydal** (coastal, Varuna, fishing/salt) and **Palai** (arid, Korravai, raiding) — each shaping livelihoods and worship. Broad social groups were **Arasar** (rulers), **Anthanar** (priests), **Vanigar** (traders) and **Vellalar** (cultivators).

**Women** enjoyed **relative freedom** — they could choose partners, and women poets such as **Avvaiyar, Nachchellaiyar and Kakkaipadiniyar** enriched Tamil literature. Yet ideals of **Karpu (chastity)** were exalted, widows led austere lives, and **Sati** occurred among some aristocratic families — revealing a society progressive in parts yet bound by custom.
keyPoints: Hereditary monarchy; titles Thennavar/Minavar; officials Amaichar, Senathipathi, Otrar, Thuthar.
Divisions: Mandalam > Nadu > Ur > Perur > Sirur; Pattinam (ports), Cheri (suburbs).
Revenue: Karai, Ulgu, Irai, Iravu + war booty; armies with Kodimaram banners.
Tinai landscapes (Kurinji, Mullai, Marudam, Neydal, Palai) with deities/occupations.
Social groups: Arasar, Anthanar, Vanigar, Vellalar.
Women relatively free (poets Avvaiyar etc.) yet Karpu ideal and Sati among elites.
